title: Why Does a Photo Have Horizontal and Vertical DPI?
description: Read horizontal and vertical photo DPI with their units and pixel dimensions. Check both axes and the intended physical print size on iPhone.
direct: Read horizontal and vertical DPI separately when a photo reports different values. Divide each pixel dimension by its matching density to check the stated print size.
figureAlt: A calculated 1200 by 1800 pixel photo at 300 DPI on both axes describes a four by six inch image.
figureCaption: AI-generated conceptual illustration, not an App screenshot or measured export. The dimensions are a calculated example.
cards.decision.heading: Start with the distinction
cards.decision.body: For ordinary photo printing, matching densities normally describe square image samples at the intended print size. Different values can suggest inconsistent metadata or an intentionally unusual interpretation. A browser may ignore those tags, so an on-screen preview is not a print-size test.
sections.detail-0.heading: Work through both axes
sections.detail-0.body: A 1200 × 1800-pixel image at 300 pixels per inch on both axes describes a 4 × 6-inch image. If the vertical density were instead 150, that axis would imply 12 inches while the horizontal one still implied four. Those are calculated metadata interpretations, not a recommendation to stretch a photograph. The TIFF specification defines separate X and Y resolution fields and a resolution unit.
sections.detail-1.heading: Use the report as a check
sections.detail-1.body: Basic single-photo DPI edits are free; advanced exports have a three-export free allowance before Pro. The reference specification explains the concept, not TIFF input support in the app. Changing a density tag does not add real image detail, and a printer can still apply its own scaling.
faqs.reader-question-1.heading: Why does the photo still look normal on my phone?
faqs.reader-question-1.body: A screen viewer can display the pixel dimensions without using the print density. Measure a proof if the physical size matters.
faqs.reader-question-2.heading: What if one axis is expressed per centimeter?
faqs.reader-question-2.body: Compare densities only after putting them in the same units. Read the physical size in the export report before sending the file.

steps.step-1.text: In DPI: Photo Print Prep, choose the intended paper size and DPI. Keep the original and check whether the available pixels suit the target.
steps.step-2.text: Export a test copy and read the app’s verification report: pixel width and height, both DPI axes and physical size. Confirm the units rather than comparing bare numbers.
steps.step-3.text: Check the file in the print workflow and make a proof if the dimensions matter. Fix inconsistent settings before preparing the rest of the order.
